This summer, The Chicago Community Trust’s Strategic Communications and Learning & Impact teams visited El Mercadito at La Casa Norte to volunteer with morning set-up and food distribution, supporting the pantry’s partnership with La Casa Norte and Nourishing Hope.

El Mercadito is a hunger relief partnership between La Casa Norte and Nourishing Hope, operating on the belief that basic human needs must be met before the cycle of poverty can be broken.

During the visit, staff split up to assist "choice shopping" and "express" distribution options, helping with everything from unloading deliveries and stocking shelves to distributing food to clients and loading cars. Together, the pantry can serve up to 150 households—75 through Monthly Choice and 75 through Monthly Express.

In addition to nutritious groceries, including fresh produce, dairy, meat, and pantry staples, El Mercadito connects neighbors with social services, referral support, and access to La Casa Norte’s broader information and referral network.

It was a meaningful morning giving back to the community and supporting the staff and regular volunteers who make this work possible each day.

Thank you for having us!

Volunteer: https://nourishinghopechi.org/elmercadito/

Ten years ago, philanthropy came together around a shared goal: support community-led solutions to reduce gun violence and build safer neighborhoods across Chicago. Since then, the Partnership for Safe and Peaceful Communities - PSPC has grown into a coalition of more than 50 funders working alongside residents, community organizations, public agencies, and civic leaders to strengthen neighborhoods through violence prevention, healing and opportunity. 

Its multi-part approach has taken shape through a range of complementary strategies, including street outreach, support services and jobs; police reform and community relations; gun policy; and community-based investments. PSPC has supported efforts such as Communities Partnering for Peace (CP4P), led by Metropolitan Peace Initiatives and provided hyperlocal, rapid-response investments through the Chicago Fund for Safe and Peaceful Communities while collaborating with partners across the violence prevention ecosystem, including Chicago CRED. Together, these approaches help illustrate how layered strategies have contributed to citywide progress.

The ruling does not mean that states like Illinois, which allows trans athletes to compete based on their gender identity, must impose restrictions on transgender students’ participation in sports.

We are navigating a moment where the educational field is moving fast on technological solutions and slow on human capacity building. This gap is highly consequential.

If our systemic leadership lags behind technology, public education will continue to be handed a future it did not design. Our most vulnerable communities will simply inherit learning structures that have been entirely predetermined for them. Equity will not pause while leaders catch up.

Systems do not transform simply because new tools or AI architectures exist. They transform when the people inside them learn to see, decide, and lead differently.

As we look toward the future of learning, we have to ask the hard questions:

What is the true purpose of public education in the Age of AI?

Whose values, voices, and expertise are shaping these new architectures?

What must remain irreducibly human?

If we want public education to evolve toward liberation rather than be bypassed, we must invest heavily in the people, the practices, and the collective spaces that help leaders make wise, equitable choices.

Through the Stay in Place pilot, The Chicago Community Trust partners with organizations like The Resurrection Project to support long-time South and West Side homeowners with resources to remain in their homes, preserve affordability, and build long-term stability. This week, Trust staff and partners saw that work come to fruition on a site visit to Pilsen. We toured a home supported through TRP's forgivable loan program, where the homeowner shared a moving story about what these critical repairs meant for her family, because without this program, the repairs would not have been financially possible. We then gathered at Dominican University to reflect on the visit and explore how efforts from accessible home repairs to broader anti-displacement strategies connect to help longtime residents stay, thrive, and build generational wealth.

Thank you to The Resurrection Project and Dominican University for hosting. Collaboration is at the heart of this work, and we're grateful for your partnership.

What does neighborhood transformation look like up close? Yesterday, members of our donor community found out when they joined The Chicago Community Trust for a neighborhood tour highlighting the Connecting Capital and Community (3C) initiative—and saw firsthand how 3C is working to expand homeownership opportunities for Chicagoans. At Inherent, we watched innovative modular homes take shape on the factory floor. Then, we stepped inside two newly built homes from 3C developer partners Nath Construction and Citizens Building a Better Community that now stand where vacant parcels once sat on Chicago's West Side.

Seeing, touching, and walking through these spaces brought 3C's vision to life. 3C unites cross-sector partners to strengthen neighborhood stability in East Garfield Park and Humboldt Park—expanding access to homeownership for first-time homebuyers through coordinated investment, policy innovation, and community-driven solutions.

"Housing stock that is affordable to working people is essential to our city," said Trust President and CEO Andrea Sáenz. "Having financial stability allows people space to plan for their future. And it is only possible to achieve this in neighborhoods that have amenities and feel safe and vibrant.”

Thank you to our guests, hosts, and partners who braved the heat to join us!

Baer led a captivating conversation tracing Chicago's architectural evolution from the Great Fire to today's skyline, noting how Chicago became "the first city of skyscrapers in the world” as well as the spirit of innovation and reinvention that has defined this city and its people ever since. Beyond the bricks and steel, it was a reminder that one of Chicago's greatest strengths has always been its willingness to build boldly and begin again. 

That commitment to bold vision and building a stronger future is carried forward by Chicago's philanthropic community. Our 1915 Society honors our donors who have chosen to make the Trust and the Chicago region part of their lasting legacy.

1915 Society and Trust Executive Committee Member Anne Ladky captured it well: “As a longtime advocate, I was drawn to the ambition and this organization's willingness to strive for bigger impact. I have seen firsthand the strengths and authentic partnerships that make this organization a vital leader in our region. I have great confidence that the Trust will continue to meet the region’s greatest needs when the time comes.”

And as Chief Philanthropy Officer Sheila Cawley reminded us: "It's your generosity and your passion that make the legacy of the Trust what it is today.”

There's a tendency to frame Chicago in terms of trade-offs—downtown or neighborhoods, growth or equity, public sector or private. But that framing misses something important. The truth is: the city works best when we move forward together.

Across Chicago, there are already examples of what this looks like in projects and partnerships that bring together capital, community leadership, and public support to create real, tangible progress. Often happening in neighborhoods that don’t make headlines for the exciting projects and innovations, but should.

The path forward isn’t just about economic growth—it’s about who that growth reaches. A truly strong Chicago is one where opportunity is not limited by zip code, and where every neighborhood shares in the city’s momentum.

No single leader can deliver that alone. It will take alignment, partnership, and a shared commitment from all of us.

Chicago’s strengths are real—and so is the responsibility to build on them. At The Chicago Community Trust, we look forward to continuing to partner with others across the city to help advance an inclusive and thriving Chicago.

The Joyce Foundation is saddened to announce the passing of Director Emeritus Carlton L. Guthrie. A Harvard-educated entrepreneur, Carlton passed away on May 9 at age 73 in Chicago. He was a Joyce board member for more than three decades until his retirement in 2022. Born in Atlanta and raised in Gary, Indiana, Carlton was the co-chairman of Detroit Chassis and SPECTRA, LLC, a group of automotive-related companies he founded with his brother, Mike. Carlton was also CEO of Magnys Innovative Solutions, an engineering firm, and co-owner and Board Chairman of HealthCURE. Carlton credited his community-oriented, “can-do” ethos to his parents, Willie and Mary.  He was drawn to Joyce’s ambitious mission of improving lives in the Great Lakes region and its willingness to take the lead within philanthropy on supporting issues like gun violence prevention. Among his many affiliations and board memberships, Carlton proudly and notably created the Guthrie Family Scholarship for students in Gary, Indiana and South Haven, Michigan. In addition to the fiscal stewardship and experience he brought to the board, Carlton also brought an unwavering commitment to mentorship, leadership development, and creating equitable opportunities for youth, and especially young boys and men of color in the Great Lakes region. Carlton was an active board member of Concerned Christian Men, which includes as its mission serving as “fathers to the fatherless.”  We extend our deepest condolences to Carlton’s wife, Dawn-Marie, his children, Carille and Adam, his grandchildren, and his entire extended family.

Financial health comes down to whether people have real choices—and too many still don’t. Trust President & CEO Andrea Sáenz notes expanding those choices isn’t the work of any one organization or sector; it will take all of us.

That’s what brought us together yesterday at The Chicago Community Trust to dig into the Financial Health Pulse® 2025 Chicago Trends Report. In partnership with the Financial Health Network, JPMorganChase, and TransUnion, we’re working to better understand what financial health looks like across our region—and how it’s changing over time.

Understanding this data, and using it as a guide, can help us advance the financial health, wealth and well‑being of our neighbors across Chicago. The data tells a nuanced story. There are real signs of progress, but they’re not reaching everyone. That tension matters—and it’s shaping how we think about our role and where we focus next.

Financial health isn’t just about how much money you make. It’s about whether you can afford life today, save, and plan for the future. It was energizing to hear about the many ways partners across the city are responding—everything from new loan products for prospective homebuyers, to flexible savings options for employees, to wraparound supports for college students.

Thank you to the Trust's Jennifer Axelrod for guiding a thoughtful conversation, and to our guests Sarah Gordon (FHN), Verónica Herrero (City Colleges of Chicago, City Colleges of Chicago Foundation), Anthony Simpkins (Neighborhood Housing Services of Chicago), and Sara Wasserteil (Corporate Coalition of Chicago) for sharing their insights.

Yesterday, The Chicago Community Trust's Income & Assets team hosted their income grant recipients for a half-day of learning and sharing.

The morning opened with informal networking and welcome remarks, followed by a data presentation on Financial Health Network insights, led by the Trust’s Learning & Impact team. The session grounded partners in what the data reveals about financial hardship and set the stage for small‑group conversations focused on reflection.

The first panel discussion was centered around the data landscape, which featured Amy Huang (UtmostU), Lara Pruitt (The Kinship Foundation), and Brittany Jackson‑Kairis (City Colleges of Chicago). Panelists discussed how data informs strategy, the benefits and challenges of disaggregated data, and how partnerships strengthen both the quality and application of data—while recognizing the limits of what data alone can capture.

Following lunch, the convening continued with the second panel about rethinking economic mobility and featured Julian Posada (LiftUp Enterprises), Pam Tully (Skills for Chicago), and Tiffany Thompson (The CAFE Group). The conversation focused on the importance of social capital, career pathways, and workplace practices, with panelists sharing what supports upward mobility and what changes are needed to better meet people where they are.

The convening closed with shared reflections and a continued commitment to learning from one another and advancing strategies that support financial stability and economic mobility across Chicago. Thank you to our speakers and grant partners for their thoughtful engagement—we look forward to continuing this work together.

Last year, we passed SB1920 to require statewide AI guidance. Now, we’re sharing how the Illinois State Board of Education can create guidance that's responsive to teachers' concerns.

Our new memo with the Illinois Digital Educators Alliance, From “Rules and Tools” to Schools, surveyed Illinois educators and found that 58% of teachers are already using AI for lessons—but too many still lack the training they need.

Read our 4 key recommendations for the statewide guidance coming this summer:

1️⃣ Statewide Vetting: Clear frameworks for safe, equitable tools.
2️⃣ Teacher Leaders: Empowering local experts to mentor peers.
3️⃣ Concrete Examples: Moving from "vague principles" to classroom-ready models.
4️⃣ Human Connection: AI to support, not replace, relationships.

💐 Ida B. Wells Barnett was an investigative journalist, an  anti-lynching activist, and a women’s suffragist. She was born enslaved in Holly Springs, Mississippi in 1862. Having been recently emancipated and living during the reconstruction era, Ida B. Wells Barnett became a prominent Black leader and activist, influencing the future of the Civil Rights Movement. 

💐 She began as a Mississippi teacher and lived through the segregation of public schools. Having witnessed the deep inequities in Black schools in Mississippi and eventually Chicago, she began writing about her experiences as a Black teacher and demanded Black students deserved equal funding and opportunities. Although she was eventually dismissed as a teacher due to her views, education remained a key part of her work towards racial equality. 

💐 She is also particularly known for her anti-lynching activism and investigations and fight for Black women’s rights.  She eventually founded several groups such as the League of Colored Women, the National Association of Colored Women, and the Alpha Suffrage Club. Her anti-lynching activism led to 20+ years of collecting stories and evidence, and she  released her findings in her publication A Red Record: Tabulated Statistics and Alleged Causes of Lynchings in the United States in 1895.

💐 We honor Ida. B Wells Barnett’s contributions and leadership efforts in Chicago and Mississippi, bringing to light to the reality of life after emancipation and the continued fight for racial equality and freedom. 

#WomensHistoryMonth #HerStory

Rosie Simpson was an Englewood parent and boycott organizer for Chicago Freedom Day in October 1963.  It was a mass boycott against CPS intentionally underfunding and overcrowding Black schools and enforcing segregation policy despite Brown vs. Board passing. There were about 200,000 students and about 10,000 parents who participated in Chicago Freedom Day. Before that, she had led a protest in August 1963 against CPS creating "Willis Wagons" or trailer classrooms in an empty parking lot as a way to 'solve overcrowding" and to prevent Black students from transferring to white schools with empty classrooms. The boycott led to CPS allowing Black students to transfer to white schools, but the fight for equal resources and funding in Black schools continued.  

We thank and deeply value Rosie Simpson's grassroots efforts for fully funded and resourced schools!

Aimée Eubanks Davis, founder and CEO of Braven, an A Better Chicago portfolio organization, is our next spotlight of Black Excellence.

Aimée is a nationally recognized leader with more than three decades of experience strengthening the connection between education and the workforce. 

What many may not know about Aimée is that she often credits her mother, Sharon Eubanks Pope, for instilling in her a deep sense of purpose and an enduring commitment to making the world a better place.

In her own words, Aimée shares a story that captures who her mother was: “The day before my older sister Rebekah was born, my mother planted tulip bulbs in front of our house in Englewood, on the South Side of Chicago, a neighborhood many call desolate. When the flowers bloomed in the spring, neighbors asked about them. The next year, they planted their own. Within a few years, the block was filled with the bright colors of tulips. That was my mother. She had a way of getting simple, practical ideas to take root. When she believed in the potential of a place or a person, she made it visible.”

That same ability to see possibility and cultivate growth is what makes Aimée’s leadership and excellence such an extraordinary force.
